Commedia dell'arte. A form of Italian improvisational theater that flourished from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, featuring masked stock characters like Arlecchino, Pantalone, and the innamorati performing scenarios with recurring plots and physical gags—acrobatic slapstick, pratfalls, and wit. The tradition originated from Italian street theater and deeply influenced European drama, opera, and comedy.

Stock characters defined Commedia. Arlecchino, known as Harlequin, was a clever servant in a diamond-patterned costume. Pantalone was an elderly merchant often outwitted and ridiculed. Il Capitano, a blustering soldier, was mocked for cowardice and vanity. The lovers, or innamorati, were usually unmasked and spoke in elevated language, providing contrast to the masked characters. Masks were iconic—all characters except lovers wore exaggerated masks revealing type and personality at a glance, allowing actors to push physicality and caricature without restraint and enabling the ensemble speed and clarity that made improvisation possible.

Scenarios, or plot outlines, were prepared in advance, but dialogue and business—the physical comedy—were improvised. Actors deployed stock speeches and gags, allowing ensemble cohesion despite spontaneity. Physical comedy and slapstick were central. Actors trained as acrobats and dancers; pratfalls, chases, sword play, and absurd situations provided humor accessible to both illiterate and literate audiences alike, transcending language barriers. Commedia emerged in the sixteenth century from Italian street entertainers and evolved into professional troupes that toured Europe. Troupes like the Gelosi achieved celebrity status and performed for royalty. Molière was heavily influenced by Commedia; his comedies incorporate stock characters, scenarios, and slapstick while introducing more sophisticated dialogue and character depth. Commedia directly influenced opera—characters, plot types, and comic situations from Commedia appear in operas by Mozart and Rossini, providing the comedic foundation for comic opera.
